title: Checkpoint: The Blue Planet
objective: After this level you can describe the size, saltiness and layers of the ocean.
summary: All Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across. Dive in: warm over cold, colors fade, light ends at 1,000 m, pressure climbs. Salty all the way down.

cards.headline: Every drop of water on Earth would fit in a ball smaller than the Moon.
cards.body: Oceans, ice, rivers, clouds: all of it. Let's build that ball, then dive into the real ocean with everything this chapter taught.

cards.fact: All of Earth's water would make a ball about 1,385 km across.
cards.context: That's about 1,386 million cubic km of water, and the ball would be well under half as wide as the Moon. Tiny next to Earth, which fits Level 2: the ocean is a thin blue coat on a big rocky planet. About 97% of that ball would be seawater.

cards.headline: Take the plunge
cards.body: Now dive into the real thing. At the top, warm water floats over the thermocline, where the temperature drops fast. A few meters down, the red light is gone. By about 200 m there's too little light for photosynthesis, and past 1,000 m there's no sunlight at all. All the way, pressure climbs about one atmosphere every 10 m, until you reach the average sea floor about 3,700 m down.

cards.headline: Salty all the way down
cards.body: Every liter of that dive is salty: about 35 parts per thousand, mostly chloride and sodium, washed off the land by rivers and pushed up through sea-floor vents. Cold, salty water is dense, which is why it settles into the deep while warm water rides on top. Size, salt and layers: that's the blue planet in one dive.

cards.headline: Chapter 1 complete
learned: All Earth's water: a ball about 1,385 km across
Warm water floats over the thermocline
Red fades first; no sunlight below 1,000 m
Pressure: about one atmosphere per 10 m
Salty all the way down: about 35 parts per thousand

questions.prompt: Blue Planet recap: if all of Earth's water were gathered into one ball, about how wide would it be?

options.label: About 13,850 km
options.rationale: Ten times too big: that's wider than Earth.

questions.explanation: USGS calculates the ball of all Earth's water at about 1,385 km across.

questions.prompt: Blue Planet recap: all Earth's water makes a fairly small ball. How can the ocean still cover about 71% of the surface?

options.label: It's spread thin: a few kilometers deep on a huge planet
Most of the ocean is hidden inside Earth
options.rationale: The ocean sits on the surface, spread thin.

options.label: The ocean is mostly ice, which takes more room
options.rationale: The point is the thin spread, not ice.

options.label: The 71% figure counts the clouds
options.rationale: It's the surface area covered by water.

questions.explanation: The ocean averages only about 3,700 m deep on a planet 6,371 km in radius: a thin layer over a big area.

questions.prompt: Blue Planet recap, from Level 8: what's left of the sunlight once you dive below 1,000 m?

options.label: Only red light
options.rationale: Red is the first color to vanish.

options.label: Only green light
options.rationale: Green fades before blue, and all of it is gone by then.

questions.explanation: Sunlight does not reach below 1,000 m; the deep ocean is completely dark.

questions.prompt: Blue Planet recap, from Level 5: which two ions make up most of the ocean's dissolved salt?

options.label: Iron and calcium
options.rationale: They're present, but not the main two.

options.label: Oxygen and hydrogen
options.rationale: Those make up the water, not the salt.

options.label: Carbon and sulfur
options.rationale: Not the most common ions in seawater.

questions.explanation: Chloride and sodium, the ingredients of table salt, are the most common dissolved ions in seawater.

questions.prompt: Blue Planet recap, from Level 4: what did the 2024 NASA-led look at comet 67P's water find?

options.label: The comet had no water at all
options.rationale: It has water; the question was its fingerprint.

options.label: Its deuterium was even higher than thought
options.rationale: Dust had pushed the reading up; the corrected water looks Earth-like.

options.label: Dust had skewed the readings; its water resembles Earth's
It proved comets supplied all of Earth's water
options.rationale: The shares of each source are still debated.

questions.explanation: Dust had skewed Rosetta's readings, and 67P's water turned out to be similar to the water in Earth's oceans.
